coverage: Japan: lost imports before intensive home-island bombing
chunk_text: At this time, in the late summer of 1944, intensive air assault on the home islands had not yet begun. But output of a number of essential items had already passed the peak, shipping losses had reduced imports of essential materials below the needs of the existing industrial plant capacity.
source_title: USSBS: Japan’s Struggle to End the War
rationale: The passage focuses on lost imports before intensive home-island bombing.

coverage: Japan: blockade-induced shortages of materials and oil
chunk_text: The blockade prevented exploitation of conquered resources, kept Japan's economy off balance created shortages of materials which in turn limited war production, and deprived her of oil in amounts sufficient to immobilize fleet and air units and to impair training. These effects were intimately associated with the political conditions culminating in the fall of Tojo and Koiso.
source_title: USSBS: Japan’s Struggle to End the War
rationale: The passage focuses on blockade-induced shortages of materials and oil.

coverage: Japan: submarine losses and blockade starve war production of materials
chunk_text: Japan's limited war production, already starved for materials through shipping lost to our submarines, was further depleted by air interdiction of sea communications as new bases eventually permitted almost complete blockade day and night. Heavy bomber and carrier raids against cities, military and industrial installations, further depleted her remaining resources, productivity and transport, lowered morale, and brought the true war situation home to the Japanese people.
source_title: USSBS: Japan’s Struggle to End the War
rationale: The passage focuses on submarine losses and blockade starve war production of materials.

coverage: Japan: asset freezing creates an economic blockade
chunk_text: These restrictions were finally put into effect on 26 July when the President issued an order freezing Japanese assets in the United States. Since Japan no longer had the dollars with which to purchase the urgently needed materials of war, the effect of this measure, which the British and Dutch supported, was to create an economic blockade of Japan.
source_title: U.S. Army: Strategy and Command, Chapter IV
rationale: The passage focuses on asset freezing creates an economic blockade.

coverage: Japan: the 1941 de facto oil embargo
chunk_text: The order of 26 July freezing Japanese assets in the United States and establishing a de facto oil embargo gave further confirmation of America's stiffening policy toward Japan. The planners had objected to the move on the ground that it might force Japan into war to gain the oil it so badly needed and thus imperil American interests in the Atlantic.
source_title: U.S. Army: Strategy and Command, Chapter IV
rationale: The passage focuses on the 1941 de facto oil embargo.

coverage: Germany: blockade-running yields only 700 tons of raw materials
chunk_text: To summarize: the U-boat blockade running system was in operations for about two years. During that time Germany received only about 700 tons of raw materials, some gold (to bolster Japanese credit) and a few blueprints and weapons.
source_title: U.S. Navy: ULTRA in the Atlantic, Chapter XIV
rationale: The passage focuses on blockade-running yields only 700 tons of raw materials.

coverage: Germany: scarce rubber and metals and blockade running
chunk_text: Germany's relatively acute shortage of rubber, tin, tungsten and molybdenum forced the nation to attach great importance to blockade running. Surface vessels were used until January 1944, but the rate of attrition made it clear to the Axis almost a year earlier that some other means of transportation must be found to supplement, if not to replace, those ships.
source_title: U.S. Navy: ULTRA in the Atlantic, Chapter XIV
rationale: The passage focuses on scarce rubber and metals and blockade running.

coverage: Germany: submarines proposed to carry rubber through the blockade
chunk_text: In April 1943 the Atlantic Section became aware of the elaborate plans for submarine blockade running through a report from Ambassador Oshima dated 31 March 1943. This mentioned a plan to convert some old Mediterranean U-boats to carry rubber and other materials.
source_title: U.S. Navy: ULTRA in the Atlantic, Chapter XIV
rationale: The passage focuses on submarines proposed to carry rubber through the blockade.

coverage: China: loss of railways prevents movement of supplies
chunk_text: The Chinese divisions, national and provincial, were spread out all over unoccupied China. Each Chinese war area contained a fair number of divisions that lived off the local countryside; great quantities of supplies simply could not be moved in Free China, for the Japanese had seized, in 1937, most of what rail net existed.
source_title: U.S. Army: Time Runs Out in CBI, Chapter I
rationale: The passage focuses on loss of railways prevents movement of supplies.

coverage: China: blockade forces local procurement of necessities
chunk_text: The accelerating inflation in China directly affected the U.S. forces there, for the Japanese blockade of China forced them to depend upon local procurement for the necessities of everyday life since Hump tonnage had to be reserved for gasoline, oil, ammunition, ordnance, spare parts, and the like. Food, clothing, construction materials, all had to be obtained in China.
source_title: U.S. Army: Time Runs Out in CBI, Chapter I
rationale: The passage focuses on blockade forces local procurement of necessities.

coverage: Bengal: loss of Burmese imports and depletion of carry-over stocks
chunk_text: After the fall of Burma early in 1942, imports from that country ceased, but exports from Bengal to areas which were more seriously dependent on imports from Burma, increased during the first half of the year. This also contributed to some extent to the smallness of the carry-over from 1942 to 1943.
source_title: Famine Inquiry Commission: Report on Bengal, Chapter XI (1945), reproduced by India of the Past
rationale: The passage focuses on loss of Burmese imports and depletion of carry-over stocks.

coverage: Bengal: lost Burmese rice imports as one contributor to famine
chunk_text: For instance, the Report suggests that the loss of the Burma rice was obviously a very strong contributory cause; but we should remember that the rice imported from Burma is about 1,500,000 tons, of which under 100,000 tons normally went to Bengal. So we cannot completely attribute the famine to the loss of the Burma rice, though it was a contributory factor.
source_title: House of Lords: Food Situation in India, 20 October 1943
rationale: The passage focuses on lost Burmese rice imports as one contributor to famine.

chunk_text: Coffee was rationed from November 1942 to July 1943. Each person got enough coffee to average less than one cup a day.
source_title: National Park Service: Restrictions and Rationing on the World War II Home Front

coverage: Exclusion: U-boat losses and convoy defense
chunk_text: The story of independents sunk by U/Boats in the Sea Frontier Areas, however, is a different story, and serves to emphasize the effectiveness of the coastal convoy system and anti-submarine measures. During 1942, of the 1,556 merchant vessels (excluding escorts) lost worldwide by all types of enemy action 512 ships or 33%, were sunk by U/Boats in our four Sea Frontiers, Canadian Coastal Zone and Brazilian Area.
source_title: U.S. Navy: History of Convoy and Routing, Chapter IV
rationale: Exclusion: U-boat losses and convoy defense.

chunk_text: But, after the German capitulation, the Netherlands Government reported the sum of about 25,000 million guilders to the Reparation Committee in Paris as damages for occupation. This would include the 8,500 million in occupational costs which I just mentioned.
